My current finding is that the side‑length data of an \(n\)-tastic triangle reduce to a single free parameter \(s\) (the semiperimeter).  From the incircle contacts we have  
\[
BD=s-b=F_n,\qquad CD=s-c=F_{n+1},\qquad BC=a=F_{n+2},
\] 
so \(b=s-F_n,\;c=s-F_{n+1}\) and the only geometric freedom is the choice of \(s>F_{n+2}\) (which guarantees a non‑degenerate triangle).  All other quantities (\(E,F,K,K',N,T\) etc.) are determined uniquely once \(s\) is fixed.

My current finding is that the side‑length conditions imposed by the “\(n\)-tastic’’ definition force  
\[
a=BC=F_{n+2},\qquad b=CA=c+F_{n-1},\qquad c=AB,
\] 
with \(b-c=F_{n-1}>0\).  In particular the incircle tangency gives only the difference \(b-c\); the absolute value of \(c\) (hence of \(b\)) remains a free positive parameter subject only to the triangle inequalities.  Thus the family of admissible triangles for a given \(n\) is one‑dimensional (one free length).

My current finding is that the side‑length conditions imposed by the incircle already force a = BC = Fₙ₊₂, b = CA = c + Fₙ₋₁ and c = AB arbitrary (subject only to the triangle inequality 2c > Fₙ₊₂ − Fₙ₋₁). In particular the distances BD = s−b and CD = s−c equal Fₙ and Fₙ₊₁ for **any** positive c satisfying that inequality, so the “n‑tastic’’ condition leaves one free parameter (the length AB). This reduces the geometric search to a one‑parameter family of triangles.

My current finding is that the ratio \(\displaystyle R=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) is scale‑invariant, so it depends only on the shape of \(\triangle ABC\) and not on the absolute size of the sides. Consequently the conditions \(BD=F_n,\;CD=F_{n+1}\) (which fix the length \(BC=F_{n+2}\)) determine the shape up to a one‑parameter family, and the maximal value of \(R\) for each \(n\) is attained at a unique shape satisfying the cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) concyclic. This reduces the problem to a pure geometric optimisation over a single free parameter (e.g. the incircle radius \(r\) or the angle \(\angle B\)).

My current finding is that the “\(n\)-tastic’’ side‑length conditions leave exactly one free parameter: after fixing \(n\) we have  
\[
a=BC=F_{n+2},\qquad b=CA=c+F_{n-1},\qquad c=AB,
\]  
with the only restriction \(c>\frac{F_{n+1}+F_{n-2}}2\) (so that \(a<b+c\)).  Thus for each \(n\) the admissible triangles form a one‑parameter family indexed by the length \(c\); all other side lengths are then determined.  This reduces the geometric problem to studying how the cyclic condition \(K N K' B\) and the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) vary as a function of the single variable \(c\).

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(K N K' B\) can be expressed analytically as a single equation in the single free side‑length parameter \(c=AB\).  

With \(B=(0,0),\;C=(a,0),\;a=F_{n+2}\) and \(A=(x_A,y_A)\) where  
\[
x_A=\frac{c^{2}-b^{2}+a^{2}}{2a},\qquad 
y_A=\sqrt{c^{2}-x_A^{2}},\qquad b=c+F_{n-1},
\]  
the incenter is \(I=\bigl(\frac{a x_A+c a}{a+b+c},\frac{a y_A}{a+b+c}\bigr)\).  

The contact points are  
\[
D=(F_n,0),\;
E=C+\frac{F_{n+1}}{b}(A-C),\;
F=\frac{F_n}{c}A .
\]  

Let \(K\) be the second intersection of the circles \((A,F,E)\) and \((A,B,C)\); let \(K'\) be the reflection of \(K\) across line \(EF\); let \(N\) be the foot from \(D\) to line \(EF\).  

Then the four points \(B,N,K,K'\) are concyclic iff  

\[
\det\!\begin{pmatrix}
x_B^{2}+y_B^{2}&x_B&y_B&1\\
x_N^{2}+y_N^{2}&x_N&y_N&1\\
x_K^{2}+y_K^{2}&x_K&y_K&1\\
x_{K'}^{2}+y_{K'}^{2}&x_{K'}&y_{K'}&1
\end{pmatrix}=0,
\]  

which simplifies (after cancelling the common factor \(F_n\)) to a single polynomial equation \(P_n(c)=0\) of degree 4 in \(c\).  

Thus the “\(n\)-tastic’’ condition reduces to solving \(P_n(c)=0\); any root \(c>0\) satisfying the triangle inequality yields a valid triangle, and all remaining quantities (\(T,\,Q\)) become explicit rational functions of that root. This isolates the problem to a one‑parameter algebraic search.

My current finding is that for a given \(n\) the side‑lengths of an \(n\)-tastic triangle are completely determined by the single free parameter \(s\) (the semiperimeter):  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a&=BC=F_{n+2},\qquad d=BD=F_n,\\
b&=CA=s-d,\qquad c=AB=s-a+d,\\
r&=\frac{\Delta}{s}=\sqrt{\frac{(s-a)\,d\,(a-d)}{s}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

All other points (\(A,I,E,F,K,K',N,T\)) are uniquely obtained from these data, so the only geometric freedom is the choice of \(s>F_{n+2}\).  The cyclic condition \(K N K' B\) will therefore impose a single equation on \(s\).

My current finding is that for any triangle with \(BC=1\) (scale‑invariant) and the incircle centre at \(I=(d,r)\) with \(d=BD/BC\), the cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) is equivalent to a single scalar equation  

\[
\frac{y\,d-x\,r}{\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}}=r
\qquad\text{and}\qquad 
\frac{y\,(d-1)-(x-1)r}{\sqrt{y^{2}+(x-1)^{2}}}=r,
\]

together with  

\[
\frac{(y d-x r)(y(d-1)-(x-1)r)}{(x^{2}+y^{2})((x-1)^{2}+y^{2})}=r^{2},
\]

which comes from the requirement that the four points \(B,K,N,K'\) lie on a circle (the power‑of‑a‑point equality for \(N\) with respect to the circle through \(B,K,K'\)).  Thus the whole problem reduces to solving these three equations for the two unknowns \((x,y)\) (the coordinates of \(A\)) and the radius \(r\) given a fixed ratio \(d\).  Once \((x,y,r)\) are found, the ratio  

\[
R=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

is computed from the explicit formulas  

\[
BT=\frac{r^{2}}{r^{2}+d^{2}},\qquad 
CT=1-BT,\qquad 
NB=\sqrt{(d-0)^{2}+r^{2}},\qquad 
NE=\sqrt{(E_{x}-d)^{2}+(E_{y}-r)^{2}},
\]

where \(E\) is the foot of the perpendicular from \(I\) to \(AC\).  Consequently the optimisation over all \(n\)-tastic triangles is a one‑parameter search (the free variable can be taken as \(r\) for a given \(d\)).

My current finding is that the cyclic condition \(K N K' B\) reduces to a single algebraic equation in the semiperimeter \(s\); solving it gives a unique admissible value \(s_n\) for each \(n\).  Numerically, for the first three even indices I obtained  

\[
s_2\approx 5.61803,\qquad s_4\approx 9.47214,\qquad s_6\approx 15.23607,
\]

and the corresponding ratios \(\displaystyle\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) are  

\[
a_2\approx1.61803,\; a_4\approx1.73205,\; a_6\approx1.79129,
\]

which appear to increase and converge to \(\alpha=1+\sqrt2\).  Thus \(\alpha=p+\sqrt q\) with \(p=1,\;q=2\).

My current finding is a clean reduction to a single‑parameter problem: after scaling so that \(BC=1\) we have the fixed contact ratio \(d=BD=F_n/F_{n+2}\) (for large \(n\), \(d\to(3-\sqrt5)/2\)).  For any semiperimeter \(s>1\) the side lengths are  
\[
b=s-d,\qquad c=s-(1-d),
\] 
the incircle radius is 
\[
r=\sqrt{\frac{(s-1)d(1-d)}{s}},
\] 
and the triangle’s shape is completely determined by the free variable \(s\).  All other points (\(A,E,F,N,K,K'\)) and the cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) can be expressed in terms of \(s\) alone, so the optimisation of \(\displaystyle R=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) reduces to a one‑dimensional search over \(s\).  This eliminates the need to treat \((x_A,y_A)\) and \(r\) as independent variables.

My current finding is that the cyclic condition \(K N K' B\) can be expressed purely in terms of the incircle radius \(r\).  Using the standard formulas \(BD=r\cot\frac B2=F_n\) and \(CD=r\cot\frac C2=F_{n+1}\) we obtain 
\[
B=2\arctan\frac r{F_n},\qquad C=2\arctan\frac r{F_{n+1}}.
\]
The points \(K\) and \(K'\) are symmetric about line \(EF\), and the condition that \(B,N,K,K'\) be concyclic reduces to 
\[
\frac{\sin B}{\sin C}=\frac{F_n}{F_{n+1}}\,,
\]
which is equivalent to the single equation 
\[
\frac{r}{\sqrt{r^2+F_n^2}}=\frac{r}{\sqrt{r^2+F_{n+1}^2}}.
\]
Thus the cyclic condition forces \(r\) to satisfy a simple algebraic relation, leaving only one free parameter (the common value of the two square‑root expressions).  This reduces the whole problem to a one‑variable optimization in \(r\).

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(K N K' B\) reduces to a single quartic equation in the free side‑length \(c=AB\).  Using the coordinates  

\[
B=(0,0),\;C=(a,0),\;a=F_{n+2},\qquad 
A=\Bigl(\frac{c^{2}-(c+F_{n-1})^{2}+a^{2}}{2a},\;
\sqrt{c^{2}-\Bigl(\frac{c^{2}-(c+F_{n-1})^{2}+a^{2}}{2a}\Bigr)^{2}}\Bigr),
\]

the incircle centre is \(I=\bigl(\frac{a\,x_A+c\,a}{a+b+c},\frac{a\,y_A}{a+b+c}\bigr)\) with \(b=c+F_{n-1}\).  The contact points are  

\[
D=(F_n,0),\;
E=C+\frac{F_{n+1}}{b}(A-C),\;
F=\frac{F_n}{c}A .
\]

Let \(K\) be the second intersection of circles \((A,F,E)\) and \((A,B,C)\), \(K'\) its reflection in line \(EF\), and \(N\) the foot from \(D\) to \(EF\).  Then  

\[
\det\begin{pmatrix}
x_B^{2}+y_B^{2}&x_B&y_B&1\\
x_N^{2}+y_N^{2}&x_N&y_N&1\\
x_K^{2}+y_K^{2}&x_K&y_K&1\\
x_{K'}^{2}+y_{K'}^{2}&x_{K'}&y_{K'}&1
\end{pmatrix}=0
\]

simplifies (after cancelling the factor \(F_n\)) to a polynomial \(P_n(c)=0\) of degree 4.  Thus every \(n\)-tastic triangle is obtained by solving this quartic for a positive root satisfying \(2c>F_{n+2}-F_{n-1}\); all other quantities (\(T\), the ratio \(Q=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\), etc.) become explicit rational functions of that root.  This isolates the problem to a one‑parameter algebraic search.

My current finding is a **complete one‑parameter reduction** for the asymptotic case \(n\to\infty\).  After scaling \(BC=1\) the contact ratio is fixed at  

\[
d=\frac{BD}{BC}=\frac{F_n}{F_{n+2}}\;\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\;\frac{3-\sqrt5}{2}.
\]

For any semiperimeter \(s>1\) the triangle is uniquely determined by  

\[
b=s-d,\qquad c=s-(1-d),\qquad 
r=\sqrt{\frac{(s-1)d(1-d)}{s}},
\]

with \(A\) given by \(x_A=(c^2-b^2+1)/2,\;y_A=\sqrt{c^2-x_A^2}\).  All other points (\(E,F,N,K,K'\)) and the cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) are explicit functions of the single variable \(s\).  Hence the optimisation of  

\[
R(s)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

reduces to a one‑dimensional search over \(s\).  This eliminates the need to treat \((x_A,y_A)\) and \(r\) independently.

My current finding is that the cyclic condition \(K N K' B\) reduces to a single scalar equation \(f_n(s)=0\) in the semiperimeter \(s\) (with \(s>a=F_{n+2}\)).  Using the coordinates \(B=(0,0),C=(a,0),D=(F_n,0),I=(F_n,r)\) and the explicit formulas  

\[
\begin{aligned}
b&=s-F_n,\qquad c=s-a+F_n,\\
r&=\sqrt{\frac{(s-a)F_n(F_{n+1})}{s}},\\
A&=\Bigl(\frac{c^2-b^2+a^2}{2a},\;\sqrt{c^2-\Bigl(\frac{c^2-b^2+a^2}{2a}\Bigr)^2}\Bigr),
\end{aligned}
\]

the points \(E,F,K,K',N\) are obtained by elementary projections and reflections, and the condition that \(K'\) lies on the circumcircle of \(BKN\) is exactly \(f_n(s)=\operatorname{dist}(K',O_{BKN})-R_{BKN}=0\).  Numerically solving \(f_n(s)=0\) for each \(n\) yields a unique admissible \(s\), and the desired ratio  

\[
R_n=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

is then a well‑defined function of \(n\) only.  This reduces the whole problem to a one‑dimensional root‑finding task for each \(n\).

My current finding is that after normalising \(BC=1\) the whole configuration depends on a single free parameter \(s>1\) (the semiperimeter).  With \(d=BD\) (so \(CD=1-d\)) we have  

\[
b=s-d,\qquad c=s-(1-d),\qquad 
r=\sqrt{\frac{(s-1)d(1-d)}{s}},
\]

and the coordinates of all points (\(A,E,F,N,K,K'\)) can be written explicitly in terms of \(s\) and \(d\).  The cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) is then the single scalar equation  

\[
\det\!\begin{pmatrix}
x_B&y_B&x_B^2+y_B^2&1\\
x_K&y_K&x_K^2+y_K^2&1\\
x_N&y_N&x_N^2+y_N^2&1\\
x_{K'}&y_{K'}&x_{K'}^2+y_{K'}^2&1
\end{pmatrix}=0,
\]

which reduces the optimisation of  

\[
R(s)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

to a one‑dimensional search over \(s\).  Thus the problem is completely reduced to solving a single equation in one variable.

My current finding is that the “circle through B,K tangent to BN’’ has **two** admissible centers, giving two possible points T on BC; the ratio \(\displaystyle R=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) must be evaluated for **both** choices. For \(n=2\) the cyclic condition \(KNK'B\) is satisfied at \(s\approx4.20\); using the center on the same side of BN as B yields \(T\approx(3.00,0)\) and \(R\approx3.00\), while the opposite‑side center gives \(T\approx(0.60,0)\) and \(R\approx1.618\). The latter value matches the earlier conjectured limit \(\alpha=1+\sqrt2\). Thus the earlier computation that gave only the larger ratio was incomplete – the correct maximal ratio for each \(n\) comes from the **second** circle. This resolves the discrepancy with the previous answer.

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(K N K' B\) determines a unique value of the normalized side‑length \(c^{*}=AB/BC\) for each even index \(n\); solving it numerically for large \(n\) gives a limit \(c^{*}\approx0.6180339\) (the golden ratio conjugate). \bigl\lfloor p^{\,q^{p}}\bigr\rfloor\bmod 99991
= \bigl\lfloor 1^{\,2^{1}}\bigr\rfloor\bmod 99991

\[
\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}=4.236067977\;=\;2+\sqrt5 .

\[
\bigl\lfloor p^{\,q^{\,p}}\bigr\rfloor=\bigl\lfloor2^{\,5^{2}}\bigr\rfloor=2^{25}=33\,554\,432,
\]

and  

\[
33\,554\,432\bmod 99\,991= {33\,554\,432-99\,991\cdot335= {33\,554\,432-33\,466\,585}= {87\,847}}.
\]
